extracted.intended_audience: aspiring satirists, poets, and students of Horace / classical Latin literature
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive guidance for composing Roman-style satire: recommendations on tone, diction, revision, audience, and prudence in personal attack. Grounded in Horace's reflections on precedent (e.g., Lucilius) and practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conciseness / Avoid verbiage
rubrics_metrics.description: There is need of conciseness that the sentence may run, and not embarrass itself with verbiage, that overloads the sated ear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep lines and sentences lean so the verse 'runs' smoothly; remove redundant or overlong phrasing that burdens the listener/reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Varied tone and personae
rubrics_metrics.description: Sometimes a grave, frequently jocose style is necessary, supporting the character one while of the orator and [at another] of the poet, now and then that of a graceful rallier that curbs the force of his pleasantry and weakens it on purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shift register and voice deliberately: alternate seriousness and jocularity, adopt different personae (orator, poet, mock-rallier) to suit the satiric aim and to modulate strength of ridicule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use ridicule strategically (not mere severity)
rubrics_metrics.description: For ridicule often decides matters of importance more effectually and in a better manner, than severity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer pointed ridicule and comic exposure when it will make a stronger ethical/corrective point than harsh invective; control tone so mockery serves purpose rather than mere abuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid gratuitous Greekisms / foreign affectation
rubrics_metrics.description: When you make verses, I ask you this question; ... choose to intermix words borrowed from abroad, like the double-tongued Canusinian. ... You could not be guilty of more madness by carrying timber into a wood, than by desiring to throng in among the great crowds of Grecian writers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not mix in learned foreign words or fashionable Greekisms merely to show learning; preserve a native idiom and resist imitating foreign fashions that disrupt clarity or national character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Smoothness and finished workmanship
rubrics_metrics.description: He flowed muddily, frequently indeed bearing along more things which ought to be taken away than left. ... he would have retrenched a great deal from his writings: he would have pruned off every thing that transgressed the limits of perfection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for polished, well-finished lines; eliminate material that clogs rhythm or thought. Be willing to cut generously in editing to achieve perfection of form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequent revision ('Blot frequently')
rubrics_metrics.description: You that intend to write what is worthy to be read more than once, blot frequently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Revise repeatedly; editing is essential. Produce work meant for rereading through careful deletion and refinement rather than hurried composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write for judicious readers, not mass applause
rubrics_metrics.description: Take no-pains to make the multitude admire you, content with a few [judicious] readers. ... It is enough for me, that the knight [Maecenas] applauds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize the approval of discerning, knowledgeable readers or patrons over popularity or ephemeral acclaim; quality over crowd-pleasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prudence in personal attack / legal and moral caution
rubrics_metrics.description: If any person shall make scandalous verses against a particular man, an action lies, and a sentence. Granted, if they are scandalous: but if a man composes good ones, and is praised by such a judge as Caesar? If a man barks only at him who deserves his invectives, while he himself is unblamable? The process will be canceled with laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid scandalous, personally libellous attacks; reserve invective for those who deserve it and take account of legal/social consequences and the standing of judges/audience. Effective satire should be justifiable and defensible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness / seize the right opportunity
rubrics_metrics.description: No verses of Horace's, unless well-timed, will gain the attention of Caesar; whom, [like a generous steed,] if you stroke awkwardly, he will kick upon you, being at all quarters on his guard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider timing and occasion—satire (and especially political or high-stakes satire) must be well-timed and cautious about the audience and circumstances to avoid backlash or missed reception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid bombast and affected grandiosity
rubrics_metrics.description: While bombastical Alpinus murders Memnon, and while he deforms the muddy source of the Rhine, I amuse myself with these satires; which can neither be recited in the temple [of Apollo] ... nor can have a run over and over again represented in the theatres.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eschew pretentious, inflated language and exaggerated claims; prefer modest, clear expression that serves satiric effect rather than ostentation.
